## Concepts
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/>

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#on-this-page
- [parameter] **Unexpected**: Packet dropped because it was not expected given the current state of the TCP connection it was associated with. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [parameter] **Challenge needed**: Packet challenged because the system determined that the packet is most likely part of a packet flood. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [parameter] **Challenge passed**: Packet dropped because it belongs to a solved challenge. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [parameter] **Not found**: Packet dropped because it is not part of an existing TCP connection and it is not establishing a new connection. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [parameter] **Out of sequence**: Packet dropped because its properties (for example, TCP flags or sequence numbers) do not match the expected values for the existing connection. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [parameter] **Already closed**: Packet dropped because it belongs to a connection that is already closed. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons
- [definition] Concepts — Last updated May 7, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#concepts
- [definition] Prefixes — Advanced DDoS Protection protects the IP prefixes you select from sophisticated DDoS attacks. A prefix can be an IP address or an IP range in CIDR format. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#prefixes
- [definition] Allowlist — The Advanced DDoS Protection allowlist is a list of prefixes that will bypass all configured Advanced DDoS Protection rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#allowlist
- [definition] Rule — A rule configures Advanced DDoS Protection for a given [scope](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#scope), according to several [settings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#rule-settings): execution mode… — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#rule
- [definition] Rule settings — Each rule type has the following settings: scope, mode, burst sensitivity, and rate sensitivity. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#rule-settings
- [definition] Filter — A filter modifies Advanced TCP Protection's [execution mode](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mode) — monitoring, mitigation (enabled), or disabled — for all incoming packets matching an expression. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#filter
- [definition] Example use case — You can create a monitor filter for a new prefix that you are onboarding by using the expression to match against the prefix. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#example-use-case
- [definition] Determining the execution mode — When you have both rules and filters configured, the execution mode is determined according to the following: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#determining-the-execution-mode
- [definition] Mitigation reasons — The Advanced TCP Protection system applies mitigation actions for different reasons based on the connection states. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/concepts/#mitigation-reasons

- [parameter] **Out of sequence**: Likely cause=Packet reordering or packet loss in the network path; Action=Increase burst sensitivity threshold for the affected colo — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/troubleshooting/#legitimate-traffic-is-being-dropped-false-positives
- [parameter] Drops during traffic spikes only: Likely cause=Burst sensitivity threshold too low; Action=Increase burst sensitivity (keep rate sensitivity the same) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/advanced-ddos-systems/troubleshooting/#legitimate-traffic-is-being-dropped-false-positives

- [definition] Implicit rendering — Implicit rendering automatically scans your HTML for elements with the `cf-turnstile` class and renders widgets without additional JavaScript code. This set up is ideal for static pages where you want the widget to load immediately when the page loads. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#implicit-rendering
- [definition] Use cases — Cloudflare recommends using implicit rendering on the following scenarios: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#use-cases
- [definition] Explicit rendering — Explicit rendering gives you programmatic control over when and where the widget appears and how the widgets are created using JavaScript functions. This method is suitable for dynamic content, single-page applications (SPAs), or conditional rendering based on user interactions. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#explicit-rendering
- [definition] Use cases — Cloudflare recommends using explicit rendering on the following scenarios: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#use-cases

- [definition] Execution mode — Control when challenges run with execution modes. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#execution-mode
- [definition] Performance and user experience optimization — Cloudflare recommends that you execute the Turnstile script as early upon the visitor's page entry as possible, so that the verification is complete and the interaction is available once the visitor attempts an action on the page. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#performance-and-user-experience-optimization

- [definition] Testing — You can test your Turnstile widget on your webpage without triggering an actual Cloudflare Challenge by using a testing sitekey. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#testing
- [definition] Limitations — Turnstile is designed to function only on pages using `http://` or `https://` URI schemes. Other protocols, such as `file://`, are not supported for embedding the widget. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/#limitations

## Log mode versus production mode
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/>

- [snippet] Enable log mode: curl "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/rulesets/phases/http_request_firewall_managed/entrypoint" \ — `curl "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/rulesets/phases/http_request_firewall_mana` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#enable-log-mode
- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-securi — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#on-this-page
- [parameter] **How it works**: Production mode=You write WAF [custom rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/) using AI Security for Apps detection fields; Log mode=You enable the AI Security Log Mode Ruleset with pre-built rules — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [parameter] **Prompt logging**: Production mode=No — only request metadata is logged; Log mode=Yes — the full request body is logged (encrypted via [payload logging](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/payload-logging/)) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [parameter] **Response logging**: Production mode=No — use [AI Gateway](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/) if response visibility is required; Log mode=No — same limitation — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [parameter] **Policy flexibility**: Production mode=Full — combine injection scores, PII categories, bot scores, custom topics, and more; Log mode=Limited — three fixed rules (PII detected, unsafe topic detected, prompt injection detected) with no score-based or subcategory logic — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [parameter] **Blocking behavior**: Production mode=Customizable — issue custom responses including custom JSON; Log mode=Default WAF block page only — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [parameter] **Best for**: Production mode=Production traffic with granular control; Log mode=Evaluation and testing — correlate prompts with detection results to tune thresholds — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#comparison
- [definition] Log mode versus production mode — Last updated Apr 16, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#log-mode-versus-production-mode
- [definition] Production mode — Production mode is the standard operating mode. You enable AI Security for Apps and create [custom rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/) using the [detection fields](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/fields/) it populates. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#production-mode
- [definition] Log mode — Log mode uses the AI Security Log Mode Ruleset — a pre-built ruleset that logs the full request body alongside detection results. This mode is designed for evaluation and tuning rather than production enforcement. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#log-mode
- [definition] Enable log mode — 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the Security **Settings** page. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#enable-log-mode
- [definition] Recommended workflow — 1. **Start in log mode.** Enable the AI Security Log Mode Ruleset with the action set to _Log_. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/log-mode-vs-production-mode/#recommended-workflow

## Prompt injection detection
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/>

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-securi — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#on-this-page
- [parameter] 1–19: High likelihood of prompt injection — the prompt strongly resembles known injection patterns. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#scoring-system
- [parameter] 20–49: Moderate likelihood — the prompt has some characteristics of an injection attempt. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#scoring-system
- [parameter] 50–99: Low likelihood — the prompt appears to be normal, non-malicious input. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#scoring-system
- [parameter] LLM Injection score: Operator=less than; Value=20 — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#block-high-confidence-prompt-injection-attempts
- [parameter] LLM Injection score: Operator=less than; Value=40 — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/prompt-injection/#challenge-moderate-risk-prompts-instead-of-blocking

## Token counting

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-securi — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/token-counting/#on-this-page

- [definition] How token counting works — When AI Security for Apps processes a request to a `cf-llm` labeled endpoint, it calculates an approximate token count for the prompt content. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/token-counting/#how-token-counting-works
- [definition] Block oversized prompts — Set a hard threshold to block prompts that exceed a certain estimated token count. This prevents unexpectedly large inputs from reaching your model. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/token-counting/#block-oversized-prompts
- [definition] Rate limit large prompts — Create a [rate limiting rule](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/rate-limiting-rules/) that restricts the number of large prompts a single client can send within a time window. This helps prevent abuse where attackers send excessively long prompts to consume model resources. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/token-counting/#rate-limit-large-prompts
- [definition] Combine token count with other detections — Target large prompts that also show signs of prompt injection — a common pattern where attackers pad injection attempts with long context. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/ai-security-for-apps/token-counting/#combine-token-count-with-other-detections

Possible values: attack, likely\_attack, likely\_clean, and clean.; Required plan=Business or above — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [parameter] _Attack_: Field value=attack; Description=Attack score between 1 and 20. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [parameter] _Likely attack_: Field value=likely\_attack; Description=Attack score between 21 and 50. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [parameter] _Likely clean_: Field value=likely\_clean; Description=Attack score between 51 and 80. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [parameter] _Clean_: Field value=clean; Description=Attack score between 81 and 99. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [parameter] WAF Attack Score: Operator=less than or equal to; Value=20 — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#1-create-a-custom-rule
- [parameter] WAF Attack Score Class: Operator=equals; Value=Attack — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#1-create-a-custom-rule
- [definition] WAF attack score — Last updated Apr 16, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#waf-attack-score
- [definition] Available scores — The Cloudflare WAF provides the following attack score fields: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#available-scores
- [definition] Rule recommendations — Blocking traffic solely based on attack score for all values below `50` is not recommended. The _Likely attack_ range (scores `21`–`50`) can include legitimate requests incorrectly flagged as malicious (false positives). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#rule-recommendations
- [definition] 1\. Create a custom rule — Enterprise customers can [create a custom rule](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/create-dashboard/) that blocks requests with a **WAF Attack Score** less than or equal to `20` (recommended initial threshold). For example: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#1-create-a-custom-rule
- [definition] 2\. Monitor domain traffic — Monitor the rule you created, especially in the first few days, to make sure you entered an appropriate threshold (or class) for your traffic. Update the rule if required. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#2-monitor-domain-traffic
- [definition] 3\. Update the rule action — If you are an Enterprise customer and you created a rule with _Log_ action, change the rule action to a more severe one, like _Managed Challenge_ or _Block_. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#3-update-the-rule-action
- [definition] Additional remarks — WAF attack score and [bot score](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/concepts/bot-score/) serve different purposes. Attack score identifies variations of attacks that WAF Managed Rules do not catch. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/attack-score/#additional-remarks

- [parameter] Content scan has failed [cf.waf.content\_scan.has\_failed](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/fields/reference/cf.waf.content%5Fscan.has%5Ffailed/) Boolean: Indicates whether the file scanner was unable to scan any of the content objects detected in the request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields
- [parameter] Number of content objects [cf.waf.content\_scan.num\_obj](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/fields/reference/cf.waf.content%5Fscan.num%5Fobj/) Integer: The number of content objects detected in the request (zero or greater). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields
- [parameter] Content object size [cf.waf.content\_scan.obj\_sizes](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/fields/reference/cf.waf.content%5Fscan.obj%5Fsizes/) Array<Integer>: An array of file sizes in bytes, in the order the content objects were detected in the request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields
- [parameter] Content object type [cf.waf.content\_scan.obj\_types](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/fields/reference/cf.waf.content%5Fscan.obj%5Ftypes/) Array<String>: An array of file types in the order the content objects were detected in the request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields
- [parameter] Content object result [cf.waf.content\_scan.obj\_results](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/fields/reference/cf.waf.content%5Fscan.obj%5Fresults/) Array<String>: An array of scan results in the order the content objects were detected in the request.  Possible values: clean, suspicious, infected, and not scanned. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields

- [definition] How it works — Once you turn on this detection, Cloudflare inspects all incoming traffic and identifies [content objects](#what-is-a-content-object) automatically. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#how-it-works
- [definition] What is a content object? — A content object is a file or binary payload in a request that Cloudflare identifies as scannable content. The malicious uploads detection uses heuristics to find content objects automatically, without relying on the request's `Content-Type` header (since this header can be manipulated). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#what-is-a-content-object
- [definition] Scanned content — Content scanning can check the following content objects for malicious content: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#scanned-content
- [definition] Custom scan expressions — Sometimes, you may want to specify where to find the content objects, such as when the content is a Base64-encoded string within a JSON payload. For example: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#custom-scan-expressions
- [definition] Content scanning fields — When content scanning is enabled, you can use the following fields in WAF rules: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/detections/malicious-uploads/#content-scanning-fields

- [definition] Paranoia level — The paranoia level (PL) classifies OWASP rules according to their aggressiveness. Paranoia levels vary from PL1 to PL4, where PL4 is the most strict level: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/owasp-core-ruleset/concepts/#paranoia-level
- [definition] Request threat score — Each OWASP rule that matches the current request has an associated score. The request threat score is the sum of the individual scores of all OWASP rules that matched the request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/owasp-core-ruleset/concepts/#request-threat-score
- [definition] Score threshold — The score threshold (or anomaly threshold) defines the minimum cumulative score — obtained from matching OWASP rules — for the WAF to apply the configured OWASP ruleset action. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/owasp-core-ruleset/concepts/#score-threshold

- [definition] Ruleset-level configuration — You can configure (or override) the following Cloudflare Sensitive Data Detection setting in the Cloudflare dashboard: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#ruleset-level-configuration
- [definition] Tag-level configuration — You can configure (or override) the following setting in the dashboard for rules tagged with at least one of the selected tags: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#tag-level-configuration

- [definition] Example — This example deploys the Cloudflare Sensitive Data Detection ruleset to the `http_response_firewall_managed` phase of a given zone (`$ZONE_ID`) by creating a rule that executes the managed ruleset. The rules in the managed ruleset are executed for all incoming requests. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#example
- [definition] Next steps — To configure the Cloudflare Sensitive Data Detection managed ruleset via API, create [overrides](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/managed-rulesets/override-managed-ruleset/) using the Rulesets API. You can perform the following configurations: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#next-steps
- [definition] More resources — For more information on working with managed rulesets via API, refer to [Work with managed rulesets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/managed-rulesets/) in the Ruleset Engine documentation. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#more-resources
- [definition] Review detected leaks — To check for any data leaks detected by Cloudflare Sensitive Data Detection, you can do the following: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/sensitive-data-detection/#review-detected-leaks

- [parameter] ddos\_l7: [HTTP DDoS Attack Protection](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/managed-rulesets/http/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#execution-order
- [parameter] http\_request\_firewall\_custom: [Custom rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#execution-order
- [parameter] http\_ratelimit: [Rate limiting rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/rate-limiting-rules/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#execution-order

- [definition] Security features interoperability — Last updated Aug 3, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#security-features-interoperability
- [definition] Execution order — Cloudflare security features powered by the [Ruleset Engine](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/) run in a fixed sequence of phases. When a request arrives, it passes through each phase in order. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#execution-order
- [definition] Features outside the Ruleset Engine — The following security features are not powered by the Ruleset Engine and are evaluated independently: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#features-outside-the-ruleset-engine
- [definition] DDoS protection — [DDoS protection](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/) is always on for all Cloudflare plans. L7 HTTP DDoS Attack Protection detects and mitigates application-layer DDoS attacks. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#ddos-protection
- [definition] Custom rules — [Custom rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/) are rules you define. They run in the `http_request_firewall_custom` phase and support actions like _Block_, _Managed Challenge_, _Skip_, and _Log_. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#custom-rules
- [definition] Rate limiting rules — [Rate limiting rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/rate-limiting-rules/) throttle or block traffic that exceeds a defined request rate. They run in the `http_ratelimit` phase, after custom rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#rate-limiting-rules
- [definition] Managed Rules — [Managed Rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/) are pre-configured rulesets maintained by Cloudflare. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#managed-rules
- [definition] Bot Fight Mode — [Bot Fight Mode](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/get-started/bot-fight-mode/) is available on Free plans. It is a simple on/off toggle that challenges traffic matching patterns of known bots. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#bot-fight-mode
- [definition] Super Bot Fight Mode — [Super Bot Fight Mode](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/get-started/super-bot-fight-mode/) (SBFM) is available on Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans (without the Bot Management add-on). It runs in the `http_request_sbfm` phase and offers more control than Bot Fight Mode. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#super-bot-fight-mode
- [definition] Bot Management — [Bot Management](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/get-started/bot-management/) is an Enterprise add-on. It generates a bot score from `1` to `99` for every request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#bot-management
- [definition] Key interaction rules — These rules govern how security features interact: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#key-interaction-rules
- [definition] Small business website (Free plan) — A Free plan includes DDoS protection and Bot Fight Mode. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#small-business-website-free-plan
- [definition] E-commerce site (Pro or Business plan) — A Pro or Business plan adds Super Bot Fight Mode, custom rules, and Managed Rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#e-commerce-site-pro-or-business-plan
- [definition] Enterprise API and website (Enterprise plan) — An Enterprise plan with the Bot Management add-on provides the most flexibility. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#enterprise-api-and-website-enterprise-plan
- [definition] Troubleshoot conflicts — When security features interfere with legitimate traffic, use the following steps to identify and resolve the issue. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#troubleshoot-conflicts
- [definition] Identify which feature blocked a request — Use [Security Events](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/analytics/security-events/) to identify the feature that blocked a request: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#identify-which-feature-blocked-a-request
- [definition] Resolve Bot Fight Mode false positives — Bot Fight Mode does not support exceptions. You have two options: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#resolve-bot-fight-mode-false-positives
- [definition] Resolve Super Bot Fight Mode false positives — Create a custom rule with the _Skip_ action to bypass SBFM for the affected traffic: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#resolve-super-bot-fight-mode-false-positives
- [definition] Resolve Managed Rules false positives — If a managed rule blocks legitimate traffic: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/feature-interoperability/#resolve-managed-rules-false-positives

## Glossary
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/>

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#page","hea — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#on-this-page
- [parameter] allowlist: An allowlist is a list of items (usually websites, IP addresses, email addresses, etc.) that are permitted to access a system. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] attack score: A number from 1 (likely malicious) to 99 (likely clean) classifying how likely an incoming request is malicious or not. Allows you to detect new attack techniques before they are publicly known. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] blocklist: A blocklist is a list of items (usually websites, IP addresses, email addresses, etc.) that are prevented from accessing a system. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] content object: A content object is any binary part of a request body (as detected by Cloudflare systems) that does not match any of the following content types: text/html, text/x-shellscript, application/json, text/csv, or text/xml. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] credential stuffing: Credential stuffing is the automated injection of stolen username and password pairs (known as "credentials") into website login forms, trying to gain access to user accounts. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] firewall: A firewall is a security system that monitors and controls network traffic based on a set of security rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] leaked credentials: Leaked credentials refers to sensitive authentication information disclosed in some way (for example, due to misconfigurations, data breaches, or simple human error), allowing other parties to gain access to digital resources. Credentials may include usernames, passwords, API keys, authentication tokens, or private keys. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] LLM: A machine learning model that can comprehend and generate human language text. It works by analyzing massive data sets of language. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] mitigated request: A request to which Cloudflare applied a terminating action such as block or challenge. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] paranoia level: Classifies rules of the OWASP managed ruleset according to their aggressiveness. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] prompt injection: The process of overwriting the system prompt for a large language model (LLM), which instructs the LLM on how to respond to user input. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] rate limiting: Rate limiting is a technique used in computer systems to control the rate at which requests are processed. It can be used as a security measure to prevent attacks, or to limit resource usage in your origin servers. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] rule characteristics: The set of parameters of a rate limiting rule that define how Cloudflare tracks the rate for the rule. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] SIEM: A Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) solution collects, analyzes, and correlates data to help manage security incidents, detect anomalies, and meet compliance requirements. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] threat score: The threat score was a score from 0 (zero risk) to 100 (high risk) classifying the IP reputation of a visitor. Currently, the threat score is always 0 (zero). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [parameter] zero-shot classification model: A pretrained machine learning model capable of categorizing data (text or images) into classes it has never seen during training. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary
- [definition] Glossary — Last updated Apr 16, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/glossary/#glossary

## WAF changelog overview
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/>

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"BlogPosting","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#page","h — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"BlogPosting","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#on-this-page
- [definition] WAF changelog overview — Last updated Aug 26, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#waf-changelog-overview
- [definition] Changelog for managed rulesets — Cloudflare regularly releases updates and adds new rules to WAF [managed rulesets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/). Updates improve rule accuracy, reduce false positives, or increase protection in response to changes in the threat landscape. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#changelog-for-managed-rulesets
- [definition] Release cycle — New and updated rules follow a seven-day release cycle, typically on Monday or Tuesday (adjusted for public holidays). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#release-cycle
- [definition] Disabled rules — Cloudflare may also add rules in disabled mode on the same release cycle. These rules make remediation logic available without affecting traffic, and allow Cloudflare to perform impact testing and performance checks. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#disabled-rules
- [definition] Emergency releases — For new vulnerabilities, Cloudflare may release rules outside the regular seven-day cycle. These are emergency releases. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#emergency-releases
- [definition] General updates — The [changelog](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/) also includes general updates to WAF protection that are not specific to managed rulesets. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/#general-updates

- [definition] Main differences — The main differences between firewall rules and WAF custom rules are the following: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#main-differences
- [definition] Improved response for Block action — In WAF custom rules you can [customize the response of the _Block_ action](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/create-dashboard/#configure-a-custom-response-for-blocked-requests). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#improved-response-for-block-action
- [definition] Different error page for blocked requests — Requests blocked by a firewall rule with a _Block_ action would get a Cloudflare [1020 error code](https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-1xxx-errors/error-1020/) response. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#different-error-page-for-blocked-requests
- [definition] New Skip action replacing both Allow and Bypass actions — Firewall Rules supported the _Allow_ and _Bypass_ actions, often used together. These actions were commonly used for handling known legitimate requests — for example, requests coming from trusted IP addresses. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#new-skip-action-replacing-both-allow-and-bypass-actions
- [definition] Custom rules are evaluated in order — Firewall rules actions had a specific [order of precedence](https://developers.cloudflare.com/firewall/cf-firewall-rules/actions/) when using [priority ordering](https://developers.cloudflare.com/firewall/cf-firewall-rules/order-priority/#managing-rule-evaluation-by-priority-order). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#custom-rules-are-evaluated-in-order
- [definition] Logs and events — Events logged by custom rules are shown in [Security Events](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/analytics/security-events/) with `Custom Rules` as their source. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#logs-and-events
- [definition] New API and Terraform resources — The preferred API for managing WAF custom rules is the [Rulesets API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/create-api/). The Rulesets API is used on all recent Cloudflare security products to provide a uniform user experience when interacting with our API. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#new-api-and-terraform-resources
- [definition] Replace your configuration using `cf-terraforming` — You can use the [cf-terraforming ↗](https://github.com/cloudflare/cf-terraforming) tool to generate the Terraform configuration for your current WAF custom rules (converted by Cloudflare from your firewall rules). - [definition] Final remarks — Any unpaused firewall rules with paused [filters](https://developers.cloudflare.com/firewall/api/cf-filters/what-is-a-filter/) will become enabled when converted to custom rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/firewall-rules-upgrade/#final-remarks

Use **Advanced Response** when you wish to return static plain text or JSON content. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-rate-limiting/#task-3-configure-advanced-response-only-business-and-enterprise-plans
- [definition] Using a custom HTML page or a redirect — If you wish to display a custom HTML page, configure a custom page for `HTTP 429` errors (`Too many requests`) in the dashboard. Cloudflare will display this page when you select _Default Cloudflare Rate Limiting Page_ in **Response type** (the default value for the field). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-rate-limiting/#using-a-custom-html-page-or-a-redirect
- [definition] Analytics — View rate limiting analytics for your zone in **Analytics & logs** \> **Security**. Rate Limiting analytics uses solid lines to represent traffic that matches simulated requests and dotted lines to portray actual blocked requests. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-rate-limiting/#analytics
- [definition] Order of rule execution — Rate limiting rules are evaluated from the most recently created rule to the oldest rule. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-rate-limiting/#order-of-rule-execution
- [definition] Limitations — Rate Limiting is designed to limit surges in traffic that exceed a user-defined rate. The system is not designed to allow a precise number of requests to reach the origin server. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-rate-limiting/#limitations

- [definition] Phase 1 (since 2022-05-04) — In phase 1 the upgrade became available to a subset of eligible zones, which had to meet the following requirements: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#phase-1-since-2022-05-04
- [definition] Start the upgrade — You can start the WAF upgrade in the Cloudflare dashboard or via API. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#start-the-upgrade
- [definition] Using the dashboard — 1. Log in to the [Cloudflare dashboard ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/), and select your account and zone. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#using-the-dashboard
- [definition] Using the API — 1. Use the [Check WAF update compatibility](#api-operations) operation to determine if the zone can update to the new WAF, given its current configuration: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#using-the-api
- [definition] For Enterprise customers — If you are an Enterprise customer, use the **validation mode** of the WAF upgrade process to check the behavior of the new WAF Managed Rules configuration. Cloudflare enables validation mode after you deploy the new WAF configuration. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#for-enterprise-customers
- [definition] For Business/Professional customers — Business and Professional customers do not have access to validation mode, which means that they will be able to check the new WAF behavior after they upgrade to the new WAF Managed Rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#for-businessprofessional-customers
- [definition] API operations — Upgrading to the new WAF Managed Rules via API requires invoking the following API operations: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#api-operations
- [definition] Possible upgrade errors — Contact [Cloudflare Support](https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/contacting-cloudflare-support/) to get help with the following errors: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#possible-upgrade-errors
- [definition] Configuring the new WAF Managed Rules using the Cloudflare API — Instead of using the previous APIs for managing WAF packages, rule groups, and rules, you must now use the [Rulesets API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rulesets-api/) to programmatically configure WAF Managed Rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#configuring-the-new-waf-managed-rules-using-the-cloudflare-api
- [definition] Configuring the new WAF Managed Rules using Terraform — Instead of using the previous resources for managing WAF packages, rule groups, and rules, you must now use the [cloudflare\_ruleset ↗](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/cloudflare/cloudflare/latest/docs/resources/ruleset) Terraform resource to configure WAF Managed Rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#configuring-the-new-waf-managed-rules-using-terraform
- [definition] Final remarks — The concept of paranoia level did not exist in the OWASP version (2.x) used in WAF managed rules. Based on the OWASP guide recommendations, the WAF migration process will set the paranoia level of the Cloudflare OWASP Core Ruleset to _PL2_. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/reference/legacy/old-waf-managed-rules/upgrade/#final-remarks

## Rule phase interactions
<https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/>

- [snippet] On this page: {"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phas — `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"TechArticle","@id":"https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/` — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#on-this-page
- [definition] Rule phase interactions — Last updated May 5, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#rule-phase-interactions
- [definition] Custom rules are evaluated against the rewritten URL — Cloudflare applies [URL Rewrite Rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/transform/url-rewrite/) before [custom rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/custom-rules/). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#custom-rules-are-evaluated-against-the-rewritten-url
- [definition] Resolution — When troubleshooting a custom rule, check whether a rewrite rule already changed the URL before WAF evaluation. You can use [Trace](https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/trace-request/) to check the evaluation order of your rules based on an example request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#resolution
- [definition] IP Access rules can bypass custom rules — [IP Access rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/tools/ip-access-rules/) run before WAF custom rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#ip-access-rules-can-bypass-custom-rules
- [definition] Resolution — If a request is unexpectedly bypassing a custom rule, check for matching IP Access rules first. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#resolution
- [definition] Skip and Allow do not behave the same way — The _Allow_ action in IP Access rules has a different behavior from the _Skip_ action available in WAF custom rules. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#skip-and-allow-do-not-behave-the-same-way
- [definition] Resolution — Review your configuration (namely IP Access rules and custom rules with the _Skip_ action) to ensure the intended behavior is achieved. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#resolution
- [definition] Page Rules do not use the same request view as modern rules — [Page Rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/page-rules/) are legacy behavior and do not line up exactly with modern Rules products. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#page-rules-do-not-use-the-same-request-view-as-modern-rules
- [definition] Resolution — When possible, migrate older Page Rules behavior to the current Rules products so the request is evaluated in one model. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/troubleshooting/phase-interactions/#resolution

- [definition] How it works — [Cloudflare Mesh](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-mesh/) (formerly WARP Connector) lets you deploy mesh nodes — lightweight network connectors that you install on a single Linux device in each network. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#how-it-works
- [definition] Step 1: Create your first mesh node — 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to **Networking** \> **Mesh**. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#step-1-create-your-first-mesh-node
- [definition] Step 2: Add a route for the first network — 1. Go to the node detail page for your first node. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#step-2-add-a-route-for-the-first-network
- [definition] Step 3: Create your second mesh node — Repeat [Step 1](#step-1-create-your-first-mesh-node) on a Linux device in your second network. - [definition] Step 4: Add a route for the second network — Repeat [Step 2](#step-2-add-a-route-for-the-first-network) for your second node, entering the IP range of your second network (for example, `192.168.1.0/24`). The IP range must not overlap with your first network. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#step-4-add-a-route-for-the-second-network
- [definition] Step 5: Forward device traffic — If the mesh node is installed on your network's router (the device that serves as the default gateway), other devices on the network automatically send traffic through it. No additional configuration is needed, and you can skip this step. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#step-5-forward-device-traffic
- [definition] Step 6: Verify your connection — Devices on both networks can now communicate through Cloudflare. To verify connectivity, try reaching a device on the opposite network (for example, `ping 192.168.1.100` from a device on your first network). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#step-6-verify-your-connection
- [definition] Recommended next steps — After verifying your connection, consider securing your connected networks with policies and access controls: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/setup/replace-vpn/network-to-network/#recommended-next-steps

- [parameter] portal\_query\_tools: Available in=minimize\_tools, search\_and\_execute; Description=Searches upstream tools by name, description, or schema using a regex pattern. - [parameter] portal\_execute: Available in=search\_and\_execute; Description=Calls an upstream tool by name with the provided arguments. - [parameter] portal\_codemode\_search: Searches available tools by running JavaScript in a sandboxed Worker. - [parameter] portal\_codemode\_execute: Calls upstream tools by running JavaScript in a sandboxed Worker. The sandbox provides a codemode proxy object where each property maps to an upstream tool. Supports Promise.all() for parallel tool calls. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#code-mode-tools
- [parameter] oauth: The server requires OAuth authentication. After creating the server, you will need to authenticate via the dashboard to establish admin credentials. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#create-an-mcp-server

- [definition] Key features — MCP server portals provide the following capabilities: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#key-features
- [definition] How it works — The following diagram shows how requests flow through an MCP server portal. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#how-it-works
- [definition] Transport — The portal accepts stateless [MCP 2026-07-28 ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28) and earlier 2025 Streamable HTTP clients at its `/mcp` endpoint. The portal selects the protocol from each request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#transport
- [definition] Built-in portal tools — Every portal exposes the following built-in tools to MCP clients, in addition to the upstream server tools: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#built-in-portal-tools
- [definition] Session lifecycle — MCP `2026-07-28` requests are stateless and do not create an MCP protocol session. The portal retains authentication, server selection, and upstream OAuth state for the user's portal authorization grant. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#session-lifecycle
- [definition] Naming — MCP server portals were previously referred to as **Agents Gateway** in some contexts. The API paths, Terraform resources, and internal codebases may still use `agents_gateway` or `agw` prefixes. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#naming
- [definition] Add an MCP server — Add individual MCP servers to Cloudflare Access to bring them under centralized management. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#add-an-mcp-server
- [definition] Configure manual OAuth credentials — Use manual OAuth credentials when the upstream provider does not support [OAuth Dynamic Client Registration ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization#dynamic-client-registration). This flow uses an OAuth application that you register with the upstream provider. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#configure-manual-oauth-credentials
- [definition] MCP Apps — [MCP Apps ↗](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview) — tools that declare a UI resource in their description — will also be available after successfully connecting to an MCP server. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#mcp-apps
- [definition] Server status — The MCP server status indicates the synchronization status of the MCP server to Cloudflare Access. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#server-status
- [definition] Reauthenticate the MCP server — To reauthenticate an MCP server in Cloudflare Access: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#reauthenticate-the-mcp-server
- [definition] Synchronize the MCP server — For servers that use automatic OAuth registration, Cloudflare Access synchronizes tools and prompts approximately every two hours. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#synchronize-the-mcp-server
- [definition] Upstream OAuth callback URL — When a user authorizes an upstream MCP server that requires per-user OAuth, the portal performs an OAuth authorization code flow with the upstream server on the user's behalf. As part of this flow, the portal registers a callback URL (`redirect_uri`) with the upstream server. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#upstream-oauth-callback-url
- [definition] Customize login settings — Cloudflare Access automatically creates an Access application for each MCP server portal. You can customize the portal login experience by updating Access application settings: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#customize-login-settings
- [definition] Manage tools and prompts — When you add an MCP server to a portal, all of its tools and prompts are available to portal users by default. You can customize which tools and prompts are exposed, rename them with aliases, and override their descriptions. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#manage-tools-and-prompts
- [definition] Turn off individual tools or prompts — To hide specific tools or prompts from portal users: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#turn-off-individual-tools-or-prompts
- [definition] Use an allowlist pattern — By default, all tools and prompts from an MCP server are available in the portal. You can invert this behavior so that all tools are hidden by default and only explicitly turned-on tools are exposed. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#use-an-allowlist-pattern
- [definition] Rename tools and prompts with aliases — Aliases let you give tools and prompts clearer names in the portal. Use aliases to: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#rename-tools-and-prompts-with-aliases
- [definition] Tool and prompt namespacing — All tools and prompts exposed through a portal are automatically namespaced with the server ID as a prefix. The format is `{server_id}_{original_name}`. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#tool-and-prompt-namespacing
- [definition] Portal-native tools — In addition to upstream MCP server tools, the portal exposes its own built-in tools that let AI agents manage server connections and discover tools during a session. These tools use the `portal_` prefix and are not associated with any upstream server. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#portal-native-tools
- [definition] Manage portals via API — In addition to the dashboard, you can manage MCP server portals programmatically using the Cloudflare API. - [definition] Force sync an MCP server — To manually trigger a synchronization of tools and prompts from an upstream MCP server: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#force-sync-an-mcp-server
- [definition] Configure via Terraform — You can manage MCP server portals using the [Cloudflare Terraform provider ↗](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/cloudflare/cloudflare/latest/docs). - [definition] Code Mode — [Code Mode](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/tools/codemode/) reduces context window usage by replacing upstream tool definitions with two tools for search and code execution. The connected AI agent writes JavaScript that calls typed `codemode.*` methods. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#code-mode
- [definition] Code Mode policies — Each portal has a Code Mode policy. The default policy is _Opt-in_. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#code-mode-policies
- [definition] Upstream servers with Code Mode turned on — MCP portals do not support upstream MCP servers that have their own Code Mode turned on. - [definition] Route portal traffic through Gateway — When Gateway routing is turned on, calls to MCP servers protected by your MCP server portal are routed through [Cloudflare Gateway](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#route-portal-traffic-through-gateway
- [definition] How Gateway routing works — When a user calls a tool through the portal, the portal proxies the request to the upstream MCP server. With Gateway routing turned on, this outbound request passes through Cloudflare Gateway before reaching the upstream server. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#how-gateway-routing-works
- [definition] TLS decryption — DLP inspection requires Gateway to decrypt TLS traffic. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#tls-decryption
- [definition] Supported transports — Gateway routing supports [Streamable HTTP ↗](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/transports/#streamable-http) connections only. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#supported-transports
- [definition] Enable Gateway routing — To route MCP server portal traffic through Gateway: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#enable-gateway-routing
- [definition] Example Gateway policy — To scan traffic for sensitive data, [create a Gateway HTTP policy](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/data-loss-prevention/dlp-policies/) that matches both the MCP server and a predefined or custom [DLP… — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#example-gateway-policy
- [definition] What happens when a request is blocked — When a tool call matches a Block DLP policy, Gateway blocks it and the portal surfaces the block to the MCP client as an error rather than completing the tool call. This applies in both directions: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#what-happens-when-a-request-is-blocked
- [definition] Connect to a portal — Users can connect to your MCP server running at `https://<subdomain>.<domain>/mcp` using [Workers AI Playground ↗](https://playground.ai.cloudflare.com/), [MCP inspector ↗](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector), or [other MCP… — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#connect-to-a-portal
- [definition] Portal homepage — When users visit the portal domain (`https://<subdomain>.<domain>/`) in a browser, the portal displays a homepage with connection details and setup instructions. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#portal-homepage
- [definition] Sign out of a portal — To end a portal session, select **Sign out** from the [portal homepage](#portal-homepage) (`https://<subdomain>.<domain>/`). The sign-out flow: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#sign-out-of-a-portal
- [definition] Connect with a service token — You can connect to an MCP portal using an [Access service token](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/service-credentials/service-tokens/) for machine-to-machine access. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#connect-with-a-service-token
- [definition] Device authentication — MCP server portals require a browser-based authentication flow. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#device-authentication
- [definition] Optimize context — MCP server portals support context optimization options that reduce how many tokens tool definitions consume in the model's context window. These options are useful when a portal aggregates many MCP servers or servers that expose a large number of tools. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#optimize-context
- [definition] Minimize tools — The `minimize_tools` option strips tool descriptions and input schemas from all upstream tools, leaving only their names. The portal exposes a special `query` tool that agents use to search and retrieve full tool definitions on demand. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#minimize-tools
- [definition] Search and execute — The `search_and_execute` option hides all upstream tools and exposes only two tools to the agent: `query` and `execute`. The `query` tool searches and retrieves tool definitions. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#search-and-execute
- [definition] Manage portal sessions — Once connected to a portal, users can manage their upstream MCP server sessions without leaving their MCP client. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#manage-portal-sessions
- [definition] Return to the server selection page — To manage your server connections during an active session, ask your AI agent to take you back to the server selection page. For example, prompt your agent with: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#return-to-the-server-selection-page
- [definition] Enable or disable a server inline — You can also enable or disable a specific server directly from your MCP client without visiting the server selection page. For example: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#enable-or-disable-a-server-inline
- [definition] Reauthenticate a server — When an upstream MCP server token expires, the portal prompts you to reauthenticate from within your MCP client. Open the provided URL in your browser and complete the login to restore the session. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#reauthenticate-a-server
- [definition] Authorize new servers — When an admin adds a new upstream MCP server to a portal, the portal automatically prompts connected users to authorize the new server. The portal batches admin changes and redirects you to the authorization flow once, rather than interrupting for each individual server update. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#authorize-new-servers
- [definition] View portal logs — Portal logs allow you to monitor user activity through an MCP server portal. You can view logs on a per-portal or per-server basis. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#view-portal-logs
- [definition] Known limitations — MCP server portals have the following known limitations: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#known-limitations
- [definition] Policy limitations — MCP servers use a dedicated Access application type (_mcp_) that does not support the following Access policy features when the server is authorized through a portal. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#policy-limitations
- [definition] After authenticating to the portal, my user receives the error `No allowed servers available, check your Zero Trust Policies`. — 1. An MCP portal and server must both have an attached Access policy. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#after-authenticating-to-the-portal-my-user-receives-the-error-no-allowed-servers-available-check-your-zero-trust-policies
- [definition] The portal URL does not prompt for authentication when it is added to an MCP client. — 1. Verify that the portal has an assigned Access policy. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#the-portal-url-does-not-prompt-for-authentication-when-it-is-added-to-an-mcp-client
- [definition] The portal returns a `522` error. — A `522` error indicates that Cloudflare cannot reach the portal's origin. This typically means the DNS record for the portal hostname is missing or misconfigured. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#the-portal-returns-a-522-error
- [definition] An MCP server is stuck in `Waiting` status. — The `Waiting` status means Cloudflare is attempting to connect to the upstream MCP server and fetch its tools and prompts. If the server stays in this status: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#an-mcp-server-is-stuck-in-waiting-status
- [definition] An MCP server shows `Stale` status. — A `Stale` status means the admin credential for the server could not be refreshed during the last synchronization attempt. The server's tools may still work for users who have their own OAuth tokens (servers with **Require user auth** turned on), but the admin credential needs to be refreshed. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#an-mcp-server-shows-stale-status
- [definition] Tool calls fail with an `unauthorized` error. — 1. If the server uses per-user OAuth (**Require user auth** is turned on), the user's OAuth token may have expired. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#tool-calls-fail-with-an-unauthorized-error
- [definition] OAuth authentication fails with a redirect URI error when connecting to an upstream MCP server. — Errors such as `invalid_redirect_uri`, `invalid_client_metadata`, or `Redirect URI not allowed` indicate that the upstream MCP server rejected the callback URL that the portal registered during the OAuth flow. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#oauth-authentication-fails-with-a-redirect-uri-error-when-connecting-to-an-upstream-mcp-server
- [definition] Tool calls fail when Gateway routing is turned on. — 1. Verify that the upstream MCP server supports Streamable HTTP transport. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#tool-calls-fail-when-gateway-routing-is-turned-on
- [definition] Users cannot connect with `mcp-remote` or similar tools. — 1. Ensure you are using the latest version of `mcp-remote`. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#users-cannot-connect-with-mcp-remote-or-similar-tools
- [definition] The portal homepage shows the wrong name or domain. — The portal homepage displays your Access organization name and branding. If the displayed name is incorrect: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/#the-portal-homepage-shows-the-wrong-name-or-domain

- [definition] Binding cookie — The binding cookie (`CF_Binding`) is an optional cookie issued when a user successfully authenticates. - [definition] Cookie Path Attribute — The Cookie Path Attribute adds the application's path URL to the `CF_Authorization` cookie. When enabled, a user who logs in to `example.com/path1` must re-authenticate to access `example.com/path2`. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/#cookie-path-attribute
- [definition] Eager redirect cookie — When turned on, the Eager redirect cookie setting preemptively sets a `CF_Authorization` cookie for every concrete domain in a multi-domain application. Access redirects the browser through each domain after the user first authenticates. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/#eager-redirect-cookie
- [definition] Allow third-party cookies in the browser — By default, some browsers block all third-party cookies in private browsing mode, including the `CF_Authorization` cookie. For XHR requests to work in private windows, you will need to exempt your application and team domain from the browser's tracking protection system. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/#allow-third-party-cookies-in-the-browser

The `aud` claim in the token payload specifies which application the JWT is valid for. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/validating-json/#get-your-aud-tag
- [definition] Cloudflare Workers example — When Cloudflare Access is in front of your [Worker](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers), your Worker still needs to validate the JWT that Cloudflare Access adds to the `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` header on the incoming request. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/validating-json/#cloudflare-workers-example

- [parameter] **Authentication model**: Managed OAuth=User-based — the end user logs in through their identity provider; Service tokens=Machine-based — a shared secret authenticates the service itself — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens
- [parameter] **Best for**: Managed OAuth=Interactive CLI tools, AI agents, SDKs where a human initiates the request; Service tokens=Fully automated systems, cron jobs, CI/CD pipelines, server-to-server communication — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens
- [parameter] **User identity**: Managed OAuth=Access knows which user made the request; Service tokens=No user identity — requests are attributed to the service token — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens
- [parameter] **Policy enforcement**: Managed OAuth=Can use identity-based policies (for example, require specific groups or emails); Service tokens=Requires a [Service Auth](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/#service-auth) policy action — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens
- [parameter] **Credential management**: Managed OAuth=No shared secrets to distribute — users authenticate with their own credentials; Service tokens=Requires distributing and rotating Client ID and Client Secret — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens

- [definition] Enable managed OAuth on a self-hosted application — 1. In the [Cloudflare dashboard ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/), go to **Zero Trust** \> **Access controls** \> **Applications**. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#enable-managed-oauth-on-a-self-hosted-application
- [definition] Enable managed OAuth on an MCP server application — Managed OAuth is available on [MCP server applications](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/secure-mcp-servers/) and allows MCP clients to authenticate users through Access using a standard OAuth 2.0 flow. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#enable-managed-oauth-on-an-mcp-server-application
- [definition] Enable managed OAuth on an MCP server portal — Managed OAuth is available on [MCP server portals](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/) and is the mechanism that allows MCP clients to authenticate users through the portal without a browser cookie flow. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#enable-managed-oauth-on-an-mcp-server-portal
- [definition] Managed OAuth settings — Configure these settings in the **Advanced settings** tab of your [self-hosted app](#enable-managed-oauth-on-a-self-hosted-application), [MCP server application](#enable-managed-oauth-on-an-mcp-server-application), or [MCP server portal](#enable-managed-oauth-on-an-mcp-server-portal). — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-settings
- [definition] Authorization flow — When managed OAuth is enabled, Access returns a `401` response instead of a `302` redirect to non-browser clients. The `401` includes a `WWW-Authenticate` header that points the client to Access's OAuth discovery metadata. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#authorization-flow
- [definition] Token format — Managed OAuth issues **opaque** access tokens (for example, `oauth:CvNoo...`), not JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). This is by design — the OAuth flow gives clients the ability to make requests on a user's behalf without exposing identity information to the client. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#token-format
- [definition] Multi-domain applications — If your Access application is configured with [multiple domains](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/#multi-domain-applications), an OAuth token obtained through any one domain is valid for all domains in the same application. — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#multi-domain-applications
- [definition] Managed OAuth vs service tokens — Both managed OAuth and [service tokens](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/service-credentials/service-tokens/) allow non-browser clients to authenticate with Access-protected applications, but they serve different use cases: — https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/managed-oauth/#managed-oauth-vs-service-tokens
